clues.title: Plate: yellow
text: Colombian licence plates are typically **yellow**.
NOTE: Within South America, yellow licence plates are almost exclusively found in Colombia.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Colombian plates are typically yellow. In South America yellow plates are almost only found here.

clues.title: Google car: short thick antenna on black car
text: In Generation 3 coverage, a **short thick antenna** is sometimes visible with a black, white or grey car. In Generation 4 coverage, a white or silver car is commonly found.
NOTE: Within the Americas, you can also find the antenna in Mexico, Ecuador and Brazil. However, Colombia is the only country with this antenna on a black Google car.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: In Gen 3 a short thick antenna is sometimes visible on a black, white or grey car; in Gen 4 the car is commonly white or silver. Mexico, Ecuador and Brazil have the antenna too, but only here is it on a black car.

clues.title: Direction sign: white metal posts, cross at back
text: Signposts in Colombia are made of white metal, and join to form a distinct **cross on the back** of signs.
NOTE: White metal signposts can also be found in Brazil, however these are usually wider.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Signposts are white metal and join to form a distinct cross on the back of the sign. Brazil has white metal posts too, but they are usually wider.

differs.how: Brazilian white metal posts are usually wider

clues.title: Kilometre marker: tall green 'Pr' or stone
text: Colombia uses two types of kilometre markers: a tall green version with the letters “**Pr**” at the top, and the traditional stone marker with black lettering. Both designs are unique to the country.

NOTE: The first two digits at the bottom indicate the road number. In this case, the road number is 90. The last two digits indicate the section of the road, which increase west to east on even numbered highways, and south to north on odd numbered highways.You can use this [resource](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anexo:Carreteras_nacionales_de_Colombia) to help identify each section.

images.caption: Tall green kilometre marker labelled Pr 28 beside a short stone marker, centre

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Two types, both unique: a tall green marker with the letters Pr at the top, and a traditional stone one with black lettering. The first two digits at the bottom are the road number and the last two are the road section.

clues.title: Pole: black-yellow or black-orange stripes

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Poles are often marked with black-and-yellow or black-and-orange stripes.

clues.title: Fence: wooden posts, some painted and pointed
text: **Wooden fences** are particularly common in Colombia.
NOTE: In addition to the unpainted variants, some fence posts are [painted and sharp](https://maps.app.goo.gl/z7gpBcspK4rCWeep8) at the top. These are almost exclusive to Colombia.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Wooden fences are very common. Some posts are painted and sharp at the top, which is almost exclusive to Colombia.

clues.title: Taxi: pastel yellow, white plate
text: Colombian taxis are always this **pastel yellow** colour. As opposed to private vehicles, they have white licence plates, which are often printed on the side and roof. If unblurred, you will often see the city name.
NOTE: Ecuadorian taxis may look similar. However, they use a slightly more saturated yellow and typically have orange plates.

images.caption: Pastel yellow taxi with a printed licence plate, marked by the arrow

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Taxis are always pastel yellow, with white plates often printed on the side and roof, and the city name if unblurred. Ecuadorian taxis are a slightly more saturated yellow with orange plates.

differs.how: Ecuadorian taxis are more saturated yellow with orange plates

clues.title: Pole: concrete, often dark, sometimes octagonal
text: Colombian poles are generally **concrete** with a variety of pole tops.
Moreover, dark-coloured poles are more common in Colombia than in neighbouring countries.
NOTE: It is the only country in the Americas, apart from Mexico and Ecuador, where octagonal poles can be found.

clues.summary: Poles are mostly concrete with many kinds of tops, and dark-coloured poles are more common here than next door. Octagonal poles in the Americas are only in Colombia, Mexico and Ecuador.

clues.summary: Páramo is alpine tundra in the mountains with very little vegetation. The best clue is the odd giant rosette plants. Most common south of Bogotá, still in the capital district.

clues.title: Landscape: hilly fields with thick hedges
text: In southern Colombia, around the city of Pasto, there are hilly fields that are unique in that they are bordered by hedges. The hedges are very thick and form very distinctive lines on the hills. It almost gives off a “British” vibe. If you are sure that it is Colombia, this is a very good meta, but such fields with hedges also occur in Ecuador.
!! In very rare cases, such hedges on hills can also occur in other parts of Colombia. !!

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: In the south around Pasto, hilly fields are bordered by thick hedges that form lines on the hills, with a British feel. Very rarely seen elsewhere in Colombia. Ecuador has such fields too, so be sure you are in Colombia.

differs.how: Ecuador also has hedged hilly fields
